name: National Dance Theatre
description: Hungary's National Dance Theatre now stands in Millenáris Park in Buda, in a converted former factory that opened in February 2019. Before that it was based in the former Carmelite monastery and church in Buda Castle, a building that had been a theatre since the 1780s.

children.text: The National Dance Theatre, in Hungarian the Nemzeti Táncszínház, is a dance venue that hosts performances by resident and guest companies. Its current address, according to its own website, is Kis Rókus utca 16-20 in Buda, and the new building opened on 15 February 2019 in Millenáris Park. The venue is separate from the Hungarian National Dance Ensemble, a folk dance company that performs at other stages.

A February 2019 report describes the theatre as a three-nave former factory, part of the former Ganz electro-technical works that the park was converted from. The Budapest firm ZDA designed it, industrial features are kept visible and a pavilion-like lobby sits partly in the park. The report mentions a 368-seat main hall and a 120-seat hall for studio productions, while the theatre's own site lists two theatre halls and a chamber hall plus rehearsal rooms. The lobby has a suspended ceiling of about 13,000 wooden pieces, and the report calls the venue the home of nearly 40 dance companies.
The theatre's programme features productions by companies such as Fitos Dezső Társulat and Duda Éva Társulat. The programme changes, so the official calendar is the place to confirm what is on.

Before the move, the theatre was based in the former Carmelite monastery and church in Buda Castle, a building with a long theatre history of its own. Wikipedia says the Carmelites received the plot in 1693 and finished the church by 1736. After Joseph II dissolved the order in 1784, the church was converted into the Castle Theatre in 1786 to plans by Wolfgang von Kempelen. The first Hungarian-language play there was staged on 25 October 1790. Sources disagree about when the dance theatre left the Castle building, so the exact years should be treated with care.
Good to know
Check the official site for the current performance calendar and tickets, since the programme changes.
Older listings may still give the former Castle District address, so use the Millenáris address when planning your route.
Millenáris Park itself is a conversion of the former Ganz works, so the surroundings are worth a look before or after a performance.

historyIntro: The National Dance Theatre's story runs through two very different buildings: the former Carmelite church in Buda Castle, which was a theatre from the 1780s, and a converted factory at Millenáris Park, which opened in 2019.

historySections.heading: From Carmelite church to Castle Theatre

children.text: Wikipedia says the site first held a Franciscan church of St John, built in 1269-1270, which became a mosque under Ottoman rule and was destroyed in the 1686 siege of Buda. The Carmelites received the plot in 1693, laid the foundation stone in 1725 and finished the church by 1736. After Emperor Joseph II dissolved the order in 1784, the church was converted into the Castle Theatre in 1786 to plans by Wolfgang von Kempelen, with the high altar turned into the stage. The first play in Hungarian was staged there on 25 October 1790.

historySections.heading: War damage, closure and the Várszínház

children.text: The theatre reopened in 1918 but closed in 1924 after a gallery collapsed, and it remained shut for about five decades, according to Wikipedia. Bombing in the Second World War damaged the building and collapsed the balcony, and it was renovated in 1947. It reopened on 13 February 1978 as the Várszínház. It housed the Népszínház until 1982 and then served as the National Theatre's chamber theatre until 1 December 2001. A Hungarian account says the National Dance Theatre began operating in the building on that date.

Sources disagree about when the dance theatre left the Castle building: one 2019 report says it was based there from 2001 to 2014, while Wikipedia says the building was the theatre's home from 2001 to 2019 and that the government took it over in 2014 before the Prime Minister's office moved in during 2019. A 2019 news report said the theatre had to leave so that the prime minister could work from the Castle. The new building in Millenáris Park, at Kis Rókus utca 16-20, opened on 15 February 2019 according to the theatre's own site. It occupies a converted former factory from the Ganz works.

name: Müpa Budapest
description: A riverside arts complex in Ferencváros combining the Béla Bartók National Concert Hall, the Festival Theatre and the Ludwig Museum under one roof. It opened in 2005 as the Palace of Arts and was renamed Müpa in 2015; its main hall is known for adjustable acoustics and a large organ.

children.text: Müpa Budapest is a concert, theatre and museum complex at Komor Marcell utca 1 in Ferencváros, near Rákóczi Bridge. Between 2005 and 2015 it was called the Palace of Arts, in Hungarian the Művészetek Palotája. It was built between 2002 and 2005 to designs by Zoboki, Demeter and Partners, and it was officially opened on 14 March 2005. The National Theatre, which opened in 2002, stands next door as part of the Millennium City Center development.

Wikipedia says the concert hall, the Festival Theatre and the Ludwig Museum were built in parallel over 28 months. The complex has about 10,000 square metres of ground area and 70,000 square metres of floor space. The Ludwig Museum's own site describes a simple, clear exterior with large glass areas and few decorative elements, and an undulating main wall inside clad mainly in walnut.

The Béla Bartók National Concert Hall is the largest section, with about 1,656 seats according to Wikipedia, although other sources give 1,699. Its acoustics were designed by Russell Johnson and can be adjusted using 58 movable resonance chambers and a suspended 42-tonne canopy. The hall's organ was inaugurated on 22 May 2006 and has 92 stops, 5 manuals and about 6,700 pipes. It was built by Orgelbau Mühleisen with the Pécs Organ Building Manufactory and is described as one of the largest organs in Europe.

The Festival Theatre occupies the eastern third of the building and seats 452. The Ludwig Museum, a museum of contemporary art, takes the Danube-facing side of the complex and was previously housed in Buda Castle. Wikipedia says the complex won the FIABCI Prix d'Excellence in 2006 and the FIABCI audience award in 2007.
Good to know
Check the official Müpa site for the current concert, dance and theatre calendar and tickets, since several halls run different programmes.
Wikipedia says the building is served by the H6 and H7 suburban railway lines; confirm the best route with a current journey planner.
The Ludwig Museum is inside the complex but is a separate institution, so check its own page for its exhibitions.

historyIntro: Müpa Budapest was built between 2002 and 2005 as the Palace of Arts, with a concert hall, a theatre and a museum built in parallel. It was renamed Müpa Budapest in 2015.

children.text: Wikipedia says the Palace of Arts was built from 2002 to 2005 to designs by Zoboki, Demeter and Partners, with the general contractors Trigránit and Arcadom Építőipari Zrt. The concert hall, the Festival Theatre and the Ludwig Museum were built in parallel over 28 months. The building has about 10,000 square metres of ground area and 70,000 square metres of floor space. It stands in Ferencváros near Rákóczi Bridge, next to the National Theatre, which opened in 2002, and both are part of the Millennium City Center development.

The complex was officially opened on 14 March 2005. Its Béla Bartók National Concert Hall has acoustics designed by Russell Johnson, adjustable with 58 movable resonance chambers and a suspended 42-tonne canopy. The hall's organ was inaugurated on 22 May 2006. It has 92 stops, 5 manuals and about 6,700 pipes and was built by Orgelbau Mühleisen with the Pécs Organ Building Manufactory. Wikipedia says the complex won the FIABCI Prix d'Excellence in 2006 and the FIABCI audience award in 2007.

historySections.heading: From Palace of Arts to Müpa

children.text: Between 2005 and 2015 the building was known as the Palace of Arts, and it was then renamed Müpa Budapest. The Ludwig Museum, a museum of contemporary art, occupies the Danube-facing side and was previously housed in Buda Castle, according to its own website. The Festival Theatre, in the east wing, seats 452, and the main lobby connects the three main parts of the complex.

name: Budapest Music Center
description: A concert hall, jazz club, music library and record label in a converted 1890 building at Mátyás utca 8. The organisation was founded in 1996 by trombonist László Gőz and moved into its own premises in 2013, presenting classical, contemporary and jazz music.

children.text: The Budapest Music Center, usually shortened to BMC, is a concert promoter, record label and music information centre at Mátyás utca 8. According to its own site it was founded in 1996 by trombonist and former academy professor László Gőz, with the aim of presenting contemporary Hungarian music in a collective and coordinated way. Its record label, BMC Records, was founded in 1998 and has issued more than 370 releases across classical, contemporary and jazz music.

The building has a story of its own. A case study by the software company Graphisoft says it began as a one-storey neoclassical residential building from 1890 with street-facing shops on the ground floor. Preparation, design and implementation took close to 10 years, and the centre opened in spring 2013. The architects were Art1st Design Studio. The original elevations were conserved and refurbished, with a new metallic corner element rising above the main cornice, and the main entrance was moved to the street corner.

The concert hall sits in the former inner courtyard and is linked to the street by a large lobby, and its exposed original brick walls contribute to its sound. The Opus Jazz Club, opened in 2013, occupies two storeys on the street side and is acoustically separated from the hall so both can run at once. The first floor holds the library and recording studios, and an attic conference room, a roof terrace and an event hall complete the building.

The Hungarian Music Information Center and Library collects and shares information on Hungarian classical and jazz artists. BMC's site says its database covers about 3,700 artists and orchestras and 33,000 compositions, and the library has more than 100,000 scores, books, CDs and LPs. BMC also says it holds about 500 events a year, only some of them public concerts.
Good to know
Check the BMC site for the current concert and jazz club calendar, tickets and any library visiting arrangements, since the venue also hosts private events.
The Opus Jazz Club and the concert hall can host separate events at the same time, so check which room your event is in.
The address is Mátyás utca 8, so use a current journey planner to plan your route.

historyIntro: The Budapest Music Center began as an organisation in 1996 and moved into its own converted building at Mátyás utca 8 in 2013. That building began as a one-storey neoclassical residential house built in 1890.

children.text: BMC's own about page says it was founded in 1996 by trombonist and former academy professor László Gőz. Its aim was to present contemporary Hungarian music in a collective and coordinated way. BMC works as a concert promoter, a record label and an information centre. Its record label, BMC Records, was founded in 1998, and BMC's site says it has released more than 370 albums in classical, contemporary and jazz music on CD and in digital formats.

historySections.heading: From an 1890 house to a music centre

children.text: A Graphisoft case study says the building began as a one-storey neoclassical residential building from 1890, with shops on the ground floor facing the street. Preparation, design and implementation took close to 10 years, and most of the transformation was financed from private resources. The centre opened in spring 2013. The architects were Art1st Design Studio. The original elevations were conserved and refurbished, the entrance was moved to the street corner, and the concert hall was built in the former inner courtyard with its exposed brick walls kept.

BMC says the building houses a concert hall, the Opus Jazz Club, the music library, BMC Records and the Peter Eötvös Contemporary Music Foundation. The Opus Jazz Club also opened in 2013. Since 2014 the information centre and library has published monographs on Hungarian composers. The Graphisoft case study adds that the founder issued a written statement forbidding future owners from changing the building's content or function, or selling or transforming it.
